answer.rationale: Constraints prune the option set before memory does: rollback_release is ruled out by compliance regardless of how well memory_b1 worked on day 18, and regional_failover (memory_b2) moves a heavy write load mid-settlement, risking exactly the in-flight writes the primary objective says not to lose. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) fits a failing downstream dependency, not a slow primary under load, and shedding at peak would drop customer writes by design. That leaves route_read_replicas and add_capacity. memory_b5 is the closest structural match to the present failure: read load contending on the primary was relieved by moving reads off it, and write latency recovered. I want its source record because the consolidated line says 'dashboard/report queries' — I need to know whether the day-55 relief came from a genuinely large read fraction or from a small reporting job, and whether it was measured at peak or in a quiet window. If it was a quiet-window dashboard fix, it may not scale to peak settlement. memory_b3 is the fallback: provisioning headroom absorbed a retail surge, but that was pre-provisioned ahead of a known window, not added 90 minutes into an active climb, so I want to check the lead time in the original record before treating add_capacity as available now. Unverified causal gap worth stating plainly: the latency climb started roughly when the release shipped 2 hours ago, and none of the inherited memories cover a non-revertible release as a suspected cause. Read-replica routing treats the symptom (primary contention) and does not address a regression in the new build; if latency does not respond, the release is the leading hypothesis and the next window should target it with a forward fix rather than a revert. Downstream value risk: shifting reads to replicas introduces replication lag, so balance and duplicate-payment checks may read stale state during settlement. That can produce silently wrong authorization decisions — availability metrics would look healthy while correctness degrades. So I am starting as a small guarded test: route only read paths provably tolerant of staleness (reporting, dashboards, analytics), explicitly excluding any read in the write-authorization path, with replication lag and write p99 both instrumented and a fast revert. Expand only if lag stays bounded and write latency actually moves.
